questions.stem: Under the Old Regime, French society was divided into three Estates. The First Estate was:
options: the peasantry
the clergy
the nobility
the bourgeoisie
questions.explanation: The clergy formed the First Estate and the nobility the Second. Everyone else, from wealthy bourgeois to the poorest peasants, belonged to the Third Estate.

questions.stem: Which statement about taxation under the Old Regime is accurate?
options: The clergy and nobility were largely exempt from the main direct tax, the taille
The Third Estate was exempt from the taille in return for military service
All three Estates paid the taille at the same rate set by the Estates-General
The taille was paid only by town-dwellers, while peasants paid the tithe instead
questions.explanation: Privilege meant that the clergy and most nobles escaped the taille, so its weight fell on the Third Estate, above all the peasants. Peasants also paid the tithe to the Church; it was an extra burden, not a replacement.

questions.stem: Soon after his accession in 1774, Louis XVI recalled the parlements that his grandfather had dismissed. Why was this decision significant for the coming crisis?
options: The parlements later used their powers to block royal tax reforms
The parlements immediately voted the crown the new taxes it needed
The parlements were replaced by the Estates-General as a result
The parlements took over the management of the royal treasury
questions.explanation: Restoring the parlements was popular, but these courts of noble magistrates went on to resist royal reforms, including Brienne's taxes in 1787, and demanded the Estates-General. Their resistance helped bring the crown to crisis.

questions.stem: Turgot, controller-general from 1774 to 1776, tried to abolish the royal road-labour (corvée) and the guilds. What does his fall in 1776 suggest about the Old Regime?
options: Privileged interests at court could defeat reforms that threatened them
The king had no legal power to change taxation without the Estates-General
The peasants rose in revolt to defend the corvée and the guilds
Turgot's reforms had already solved the crown's financial problems
questions.explanation: Turgot's reforms provoked opposition from the parlements, the guilds and courtiers, and Louis XVI dismissed him. The episode shows how privileged groups could block change and how the king lacked the resolve to back his ministers.

questions.stem: France's involvement in the American War of Independence contributed to the revolution mainly because:
options: it was paid for largely by borrowing, sharply increasing royal debt
France lost the war and was forced to pay compensation to Britain
it was funded by a new tax on noble land approved by the parlements
it ended France's trade with its Caribbean colonies for a generation
questions.explanation: France helped secure American independence, but the war was financed mainly with loans, so debt repayments came to consume a large share of royal revenue. Returning soldiers also brought back ideas about liberty and representation.

questions.stem: In 1781 Jacques Necker published the 'Compte rendu au roi'. Why did it make the later financial crisis harder to manage?
options: It revealed a huge deficit and caused an immediate run on the royal treasury
It proposed abolishing noble tax privileges, which united the nobles against him
It was suppressed by the king, so the public learned nothing of royal finances
It claimed a surplus, so later warnings of a deficit were doubted
questions.explanation: Necker's account showed a surplus in the ordinary budget while leaving out the extraordinary costs of war. When Calonne later revealed a large deficit, many doubted him and blamed ministerial mismanagement. It was published, not suppressed, and it hid the deficit rather than revealing it.

questions.stem: In 1787 Calonne put his reform plan, including a universal land tax, to an Assembly of Notables. What was the result?
options: The Notables refused to approve it and Calonne was dismissed
The Notables approved it and the deficit was quickly closed
The Notables voted to abolish the monarchy and summon a republic
The Notables accepted it on condition that Necker be dismissed
questions.explanation: The Notables, drawn mainly from the privileged orders, would not accept a tax that touched their privileges and argued only a wider body could consent to it. Calonne fell in April 1787 and was replaced by Loménie de Brienne.

questions.stem: The study design calls 1787–88 the 'revolt of the Notables'. Which development best fits this description?
options: Paris crowds attacked the Bastille to seize gunpowder for their defence
Third Estate deputies declared themselves the National Assembly at Versailles
Privileged bodies such as the parlements resisted royal reforms and demanded the Estates-General
Peasants burned manorial records across the provinces in protest at seigneurial dues and the tithe
questions.explanation: In 1787–88 the challenge to royal authority came from the privileged: the Notables, then the parlements, refused reforms and called for the Estates-General. Burning manorial records was the Great Fear and the Bastille was stormed in 1789, after popular forces had entered the revolution.

questions.stem: During a royal session in November 1787, the Duke of Orléans called a royal decree illegal. Louis XVI is recorded as replying, in effect, 'It is legal because I wish it.' This exchange illustrates:
options: a clash between absolute royal power and claims that law limited it
the king's acceptance that the parlements held the final power over taxation
the alliance between the king and the Duke of Orléans against the parlements
the influence of Rousseau's general will on Louis XVI's own political thinking
questions.explanation: The reply expresses the principle of absolute monarchy, that law flows from the king's will. Orléans' challenge reflects the growing claim, voiced by the parlements, that royal power was bound by law and consent. It shows conflict, not an alliance or acceptance.

questions.stem: The 'Day of Tiles' (June 1788) took place in Grenoble when:
options: Paris crowds tore up roof tiles to build barricades against the king's army
peasants attacked a tax office and destroyed its records with burning tiles
deputies of the Third Estate met in a tiled hall and swore an oath
townspeople pelted royal troops from rooftops over the parlement's exile
questions.explanation: When troops were sent to Grenoble over the May Edicts, which stripped the parlements of power, townspeople pelted them from the rooftops. The defiance in Dauphiné led to the Vizille assembly, which demanded the Estates-General with a doubled Third Estate.

questions.stem: In August 1788 the royal treasury suspended payments. What did Louis XVI do in response?
options: He accepted Calonne's land tax and had it registered by force
He confirmed the Estates-General for 1789 and recalled Necker
He dissolved the parlements and ruled through military governors
He declared war on Britain to restore the crown's prestige
questions.explanation: With the treasury effectively bankrupt, Brienne resigned; the king recalled the popular Necker and confirmed that the Estates-General would meet in 1789. This turned the financial crisis into a political one.

questions.stem: In September 1788 the Parlement of Paris ruled that the Estates-General should meet in the form of 1614. Why did this ruling cost the parlement its popularity?
options: Meeting as in 1614 meant voting by order, letting the clergy and nobles outvote the Third
Meeting as in 1614 meant giving the king a veto over every decision of the Estates
Meeting as in 1614 meant excluding all Third Estate deputies from the assembly
Meeting as in 1614 meant the Estates could discuss only the royal budget and nothing else
questions.explanation: In 1614 each order met and voted separately with equal numbers, so the two privileged orders could always outvote the Third Estate. Patriots who had seen the parlement as a defender of liberty now saw it as defending privilege.

questions.stem: In December 1788 the royal council agreed to double the number of Third Estate deputies. Why did this not settle the dispute?
options: It required Third Estate deputies to be chosen by the nobility
It did not decide whether the Estates would vote by order or by head
It doubled the clergy and nobility as well, keeping the old balance
It applied only to the elections held in Paris and not the provinces
questions.explanation: Doubling the Third gave it as many deputies as the other two orders combined, but this mattered only if votes were counted by head. The question of voting was left open, and it became the first conflict when the Estates met in May 1789.

questions.stem: The 'cahiers de doléances' of 1789 were:
options: lists of grievances drawn up across France for the Estates-General
pamphlets written by Sieyès attacking the privileges of the nobility
royal decrees calling the deputies to meet at Versailles in May
newspapers printed by the National Assembly to report its debates
questions.explanation: Each order, and many local communities, drew up cahiers listing their grievances and hopes for reform. They are a key source for opinion on the eve of the revolution; Sieyès's work was a separate pamphlet.

questions.stem: Historians reading the cahiers de doléances of the Third Estate generally find that they:
options: were loyal to the king but asked for fairer taxes and regular Estates
demanded the abolition of the monarchy and the creation of a republic
called for the execution of the king's ministers and leading nobles
rejected the Estates-General and asked the king to govern alone
questions.explanation: The cahiers were overwhelmingly loyal to the monarchy; they blamed ministers and privilege, and asked for fairer taxes, an end to abuses and regular meetings of the Estates-General. Republican demands are almost absent in 1789.

questions.stem: Sieyès's pamphlet 'What is the Third Estate?' (January 1789) answered its title question with:
options: 'Everything'
'Nothing'
'Something'
'The nation's servant'
questions.explanation: Sieyès asked three questions: what is the Third Estate (everything), what has it been in the political order (nothing), and what does it want to be (something). The other answers belong to the later questions, not the first.

questions.stem: In 'What is the Third Estate?', Sieyès argued that the privileged orders were:
options: outside the nation, a burden the Third Estate could do without
the natural leaders of the nation who deserved their privileges
equal partners with the Third Estate in a single assembly
servants of the king who should be paid from the royal treasury
questions.explanation: Sieyès claimed the Third Estate did the nation's useful work and formed a complete nation by itself, while the privileged orders were alien to it. This was a direct attack on privilege and gave the Third's deputies a justification for acting alone.

questions.stem: Why did political pamphlets have such influence in 1788–89?
options: The crown paid pamphleteers to promote the abolition of noble privilege
Pamphlets were read aloud in the Estates-General as official reports
Only nobles could read, so pamphlets spread mainly through the court
Censorship relaxed when the crown invited views on the Estates-General
questions.explanation: When the government invited opinions on how the Estates-General should be organised, censorship loosened and thousands of pamphlets appeared. Read aloud and discussed in cafés and clubs, they spread ideas well beyond the literate.

questions.stem: Why did the harvest crisis of 1788–89 increase unrest in Paris?
options: Food shortages led the nobility to cancel all seigneurial dues
Bread prices rose sharply, leaving workers with little money for anything else
Peasants flooded Paris with cheap grain, ruining the city's bakers
The crown banned bread sales in Paris to feed the army
questions.explanation: Hail and a poor harvest in 1788, then a severe winter, drove bread prices to a peak in July 1789. Bread was the staple of Parisian workers, so dearer bread meant hunger and less spending on manufactures, which also cut jobs.

questions.stem: The Réveillon riots of April 1789 broke out in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine after:
options: rumours spread that aristocrats had hired brigands to burn the harvest
a manufacturer was reported to have said workers could live on less
the king dismissed Necker and ordered troops to surround Paris
the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly at Versailles
questions.explanation: Réveillon's remark about wages, made amid high bread prices, led crowds to sack his house and factory; troops fired and many were killed. Necker's dismissal and the Assembly's declaration came later, and the brigand rumours belong to the Great Fear.

questions.stem: On 17 June 1789 the Third Estate:
options: declared itself the National Assembly
swore the Tennis Court Oath
stormed the Bastille
abolished the feudal regime
questions.explanation: On 17 June, on Sieyès's motion, the Third Estate claimed to represent the nation and took the name National Assembly. The Tennis Court Oath followed on 20 June, the Bastille on 14 July, and the abolition of feudalism on 4 August.

questions.stem: In the Tennis Court Oath of 20 June 1789, the deputies swore:
options: to take up arms to defend Paris against the royal army
to abolish the nobility and confiscate the lands of the Church
not to separate until they had given France a constitution
to remain loyal to the king and accept his decision on voting
questions.explanation: Locked out of their hall, the deputies met in a nearby tennis court and swore not to separate until a constitution was established. The oath claimed sovereign authority for the Assembly against the king.

questions.stem: At the royal session of 23 June 1789, Louis XVI offered some reforms but annulled the Third Estate's decrees and ordered the orders to meet separately. What happened next?
options: The deputies obeyed, and the Estates-General met as three separate orders until mid-July
The king dissolved the Estates-General and arrested its leaders
The nobility joined the Third Estate and the clergy left Versailles
The deputies refused to leave, and the king soon ordered all to join them
questions.explanation: The Third's deputies stayed in the hall, majorities of the clergy and some liberal nobles joined them, and on 27 June the king ordered the remaining deputies to join the National Assembly. Meanwhile he gathered troops near Paris, which alarmed the city.

questions.stem: What immediate event in July 1789 convinced many Parisians that the king planned to crush the National Assembly by force?
options: The night of 4 August, when the Assembly abolished privilege
The dismissal of Necker on 11 July, as troops gathered around Paris
The Day of Tiles in Grenoble, which led to fighting with royal troops
The publication of Sieyès's pamphlet on the Third Estate
questions.explanation: Necker's dismissal, together with troops concentrated near Paris, was taken as the start of a royal counter-stroke. Crowds armed themselves, sought weapons at the Invalides and on 14 July stormed the Bastille. The other events came earlier or later.

questions.stem: Why did the crowd attack the Bastille on 14 July 1789?
options: To free the hundreds of political prisoners held in its cells
To capture the king, who was staying in the fortress
To destroy the tax records of the Farmers-General kept there
To seize gunpowder stored there to defend Paris against royal troops
questions.explanation: The crowd already had muskets from the Invalides and needed the powder held in the Bastille. The fortress held only seven prisoners; it mattered more as a symbol of royal despotism than as a prison.

questions.stem: Which was a direct consequence of the fall of the Bastille in July 1789?
options: The Assembly of Notables was recalled to vote new taxes
Louis XVI recalled Necker and accepted the tricolour cockade in Paris
Louis XVI fled Paris for the Austrian border with his family
The National Assembly declared France a republic
questions.explanation: Faced with a city in arms and unreliable troops, the king withdrew the soldiers, recalled Necker and visited Paris on 17 July, where he accepted the tricolour cockade. Paris gained a new municipal government under Bailly and a National Guard under Lafayette. The flight came in 1791, the republic in 1792.

questions.stem: During the 'Great Fear' of late July and early August 1789, peasants:
options: elected deputies to the Estates-General and wrote their cahiers
joined the royal army to restore order in the provinces
armed against rumoured brigands and burned manorial records in châteaux
marched on Versailles and brought the royal family back to Paris in triumph
questions.explanation: Rumours of an aristocratic plot and brigands set off panic; armed peasants turned on seigneurs and burned the records of feudal dues. The march to Versailles was the October Days, after the period of this area of study.

questions.stem: On the night of 4 August 1789, liberal nobles proposed giving up feudal privileges. Historians usually explain their action mainly as:
options: a plan to force the clergy to pay for the war with Britain
a reaction to Sieyès's demand for the execution of the nobility
a response to peasant violence, intended to restore order in the countryside
a response to the king's order that all privileges be abolished
questions.explanation: Faced with the risings of the Great Fear, deputies hoped that renouncing privileges would calm the countryside. The king gave no such order, and Sieyès never demanded executions.

questions.stem: Which statement about the decrees that followed the night of 4 August 1789 is accurate?
options: Every seigneurial due was abolished at once, with nothing owed by the peasants
The tithe was kept, but noble hunting rights and seigneurial courts were abolished
Noble privileges were abolished, but the sale of public offices was kept in place
Personal servitude ended outright, but many dues on land were to be bought out
questions.explanation: The decrees declared the feudal regime abolished, ending personal dues such as serfdom without compensation, but dues attached to property were to be redeemed. The tithe and venal offices were in fact abolished. Peasants resented the redemption payments, which were finally cancelled in 1793.

questions.stem: Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748) challenged absolute authority by arguing that:
options: liberty is best protected by separating legislative, executive and judicial power
sovereignty belongs to the general will of the whole people
the Church should be abolished and replaced by a religion of reason
the nation's wealth comes from land, so only land should be taxed
questions.explanation: Montesquieu argued that liberty depends on dividing power so that no one body holds all of it. The general will is Rousseau's idea, and the single tax on land was the physiocrats'. Montesquieu's ideas were used by the parlements to resist royal 'despotism'.

questions.stem: Rousseau's 'The Social Contract' (1762) contributed to revolutionary thinking chiefly through the idea that:
options: the king's power is limited by the ancient privileges of the parlements
power must be shared between a king, a nobility and the people
the Church is the necessary foundation of all lawful government
the people are sovereign and law should express the general will
questions.explanation: Rousseau located sovereignty in the people, whose general will should make the law. Revolutionaries drew on this to claim popular sovereignty; the idea of limits through intermediary bodies such as the parlements is closer to Montesquieu.

questions.stem: Voltaire's attacks on the Catholic Church, such as his campaign over the Calas affair, mainly targeted:
options: the doctrine that all people are born equal in natural rights
the separation of powers between the king and the parlements
the theory that a nation's wealth comes only from its land
religious intolerance and the Church's power over thought and justice
questions.explanation: Voltaire campaigned against intolerance and fanaticism, notably in defending the memory of Jean Calas, a Protestant executed after an unjust trial. His work undermined the Church's authority, part of the Enlightenment attack on the Church.

questions.stem: In Beaumarchais's comedy 'The Marriage of Figaro', first performed in 1784, the servant Figaro mocks his noble master for having taken the trouble to be born and nothing more. Which Enlightenment criticism does this express?
options: The critique of the physiocrats' theory of the land tax
The critique of privilege based on birth rather than merit
The critique of absolute royal authority over the courts
The critique of the Church's ownership of land and tithes
questions.explanation: Figaro's jibe attacks the idea that birth alone entitles nobles to rank and privilege. It targets the nobility, not the king or the Church, and its popularity with aristocratic audiences shows how far such ideas had spread.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes the critique of privilege from the claim to popular sovereignty?
options: One was voiced only by liberal nobles; the other only by peasants and urban workers
One concerned taxes on land; the other concerned trade and manufacturing
One attacked rights based on birth; the other placed final authority in the nation
One demanded an end to the monarchy; the other demanded an end to the Church
questions.explanation: The critique of privilege challenged a society of orders in which birth brought legal and fiscal advantages. Popular sovereignty answered a different question, who holds supreme authority, by placing it in the nation rather than the king. Neither demanded an end to the monarchy in 1789.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Louis XVI's contribution to the outbreak of revolution?
options: His harsh repression of the parlements in 1774 provoked a noble rebellion
His decision to declare war on Austria in 1789 bankrupted the treasury
His refusal ever to call the Estates-General left the Third Estate no outlet
His indecision and changes of course weakened reform and his authority
questions.explanation: Louis XVI appointed reforming ministers and then abandoned them, gave way to pressure, and alternated concession with shows of force, as in June and July 1789. He restored rather than repressed the parlements, and he did call the Estates-General.

questions.stem: The Diamond Necklace Affair (1785–86) damaged the monarchy because:
options: it revealed that the queen was secretly funding Austria's army
the public believed the queen was involved, though she was innocent
the queen was convicted of fraud by the Parlement of Paris
the king used treasury funds to buy the necklace for the queen
questions.explanation: Marie Antoinette had no part in the fraud, but when the Parlement acquitted Cardinal de Rohan, many believed the worst of her. The affair fed pamphlets attacking her reputation and with it the monarchy's.

questions.stem: A student writes that Marie Antoinette provoked the revolution by saying of the hungry poor, 'Let them eat cake.' The best evaluation of this claim is that:
options: it is accurate, and the remark was recorded in the cahiers of the Third Estate
it is accurate, and Sieyès quoted the remark in 'What is the Third Estate?'
it is accurate, and the remark was the direct cause of the Réveillon riots
there is no reliable evidence she said it; it reflects hostile images of her
questions.explanation: The phrase appears in Rousseau's 'Confessions', attributed to an unnamed princess, when Marie Antoinette was a child, and there is no reliable evidence she said it. Its later attribution to her reveals hostile popular images of the queen, not her actual words.

questions.stem: Why was Jacques Necker so popular with the Third Estate by 1789?
options: He wrote 'What is the Third Estate?' and demanded voting by head
He commanded the troops who refused to fire on the Paris crowds
He was seen as an honest reformer whose recall in 1788 raised hopes
He was a noble who had led the Assembly of Notables against the crown
questions.explanation: Necker, a Protestant banker from Geneva, had a reputation for sound finance, and his recall in 1788 seemed a promise of reform. That is why his dismissal on 11 July 1789 caused such alarm in Paris. Sieyès, not Necker, wrote the pamphlet.

questions.stem: How did the Marquis de Lafayette contribute to the outbreak of revolution in 1789?
options: He presented a draft declaration of rights and led the Paris National Guard
He led the royal troops that surrounded Paris in July and was later dismissed
He drafted the cahier of the clergy and led the clergy over to the Third Estate
He proposed the universal land tax to the Assembly of Notables
questions.explanation: Lafayette, a liberal noble who had fought in America, presented a draft declaration of rights in July 1789 and on 15 July was made commander of the new Paris National Guard. The land tax was Calonne's proposal.

questions.stem: Which group's actions in 1787–88 are best described as both challenging royal authority and defending privilege?
options: The nobility and the parlements
The urban workers of Paris
The peasants of the provinces
The Third Estate deputies
questions.explanation: The nobles and parlements resisted royal 'despotism' in the name of liberty, but much of their resistance aimed to protect their own fiscal privileges, as the ruling for the forms of 1614 revealed. The other groups challenged privilege rather than defending it.

questions.stem: The Third Estate's deputies to the Estates-General were drawn mostly from:
options: the professional bourgeoisie, especially lawyers and officials
peasant farmers elected directly by their villages
urban workers and artisans from Paris
merchants and bankers from the Atlantic ports
questions.explanation: Lawyers and office-holders formed the largest group among Third Estate deputies, which is why the revolution's early leadership was largely professional and bourgeois. Peasants and workers were represented by these men, not by members of their own class.

questions.stem: What role did the urban workers of Paris play in the revolution of 1789?
options: They opposed the National Assembly and supported the royal troops around Paris
Their action, as at the Bastille, shielded the Assembly from the king's troops
They led the Assembly of Notables in refusing the land tax
They elected most of the deputies of the clergy and nobility
questions.explanation: Artisans and workers of quarters such as the Faubourg Saint-Antoine were prominent in the taking of the Bastille, which forced the king to withdraw his troops and so saved the Assembly. Popular action gave the deputies' claims real force.

questions.stem: Georges Lefebvre, in 'The Coming of the French Revolution', argued that 1789 involved four revolutions. Which list matches his interpretation?
options: Aristocratic, bourgeois, popular (urban) and peasant
Financial, military, religious and diplomatic
Royal, aristocratic, clerical and bourgeois
Political, cultural, economic and environmental
questions.explanation: Lefebvre, a leading historian in the Marxist tradition, saw an aristocratic revolt opening the way for a bourgeois revolution, which was saved by urban and peasant revolutions. His scheme made social classes the actors of 1789.

questions.stem: Revisionist historian Alfred Cobban challenged the Marxist interpretation of 1789 by arguing that:
options: the revolution was caused by peasants seeking to abolish private property
the revolution began as a plot by the king to destroy the parlements
the revolution was led by a rising capitalist class against feudal nobles
the men of 1789 were mainly lawyers and officials, not capitalists
questions.explanation: Cobban argued that the men of 1789 were mostly office-holders and professionals rather than a capitalist class, undermining the idea of a bourgeois revolution against feudalism. The final option states the Marxist view he attacked.
